cards.body: A core loop is the 30-second cycle the player repeats hundreds of times: spot enemy, aim, shoot, loot, repeat. If the loop isn't fun in minute one, no amount of content will save it. Design the loop first, build everything around it.
cards.title: The core loop is the whole game

cards.body: Extrinsic motivation is points, ranks, skins — rewards the game hands you. Intrinsic is mastery, curiosity, expression — rewards you give yourself. Extrinsic gets players through the door; intrinsic keeps them for a thousand hours.
cards.title: Intrinsic beats extrinsic

cards.body: Great games teach their hook in the first minute with zero tutorial: Portal hands you a gun and a wall. Vampire Survivors throws enemies at you and the XP gems do the teaching. Ask yourself: what does the player DO in minute one — and is it already fun?

Steal loops, never steal games. Don't clone a hit — extract its loop. 'Explore, fight, get stronger, explore deeper' powers Zelda and Hades alike. Your originality goes into the theme, the feel, and your twist on the loop.

choices: The 30-second action cycle the player repeats
cards.explain: The core loop is the repeating heartbeat of play — spot, aim, shoot, loot. Everything else in the game serves it.

choices: If the loop isn't fun, no content will save the game
questions.explain: Content is fuel; the loop is the engine. A boring loop with great content is still boring.
questions.q: Why design the core loop before anything else?

choices: The satisfaction of mastering a hard boss
questions.explain: Mastery comes from within — nobody hands it to you. Bonuses and ranks are extrinsic rewards.

choices: Letting the player do the fun thing in minute one
questions.explain: Portal gives you the gun and a wall. Players learn by doing, not by reading.
questions.q: A game teaches its hook best by…

choices: Copy its art and levels exactly
Extract its core loop and twist the theme
Use the same title with a 2
questions.explain: Loops are reusable design patterns; copying the whole game is cloning. Originality lives in theme, feel, and twist.
questions.q: What's the smart way to borrow from a hit game?

choices: Keeping players for a thousand hours
questions.explain: Points and loot are great bait. Long-term retention comes from intrinsic drive — mastery and curiosity.

flashcards.back: The short action cycle the player repeats constantly — the heartbeat of the game.
Drive from within: mastery, curiosity, self-expression. Keeps players for years.
Drive from rewards: points, ranks, loot. Gets players through the door.
The fun the player feels in the first 60 seconds — no tutorial needed.

cards.body: Good difficulty rises like a ramp: teach a skill, test it, then combine it with an old one. Spikes frustrate, flatlines bore. Aim for the flow channel — the sweet spot between anxiety and boredom.
cards.title: Difficulty is a curve, not a wall

cards.body: A choice with no downside is no choice at all. Risk/reward is the engine of tension: push for the risky shortcut or play it safe? Dead Cells turns every door into a gamble — heal now, or risk the next biome for better loot?
cards.title: Risk/reward makes choices meaningful

cards.body: Juice is the secret sauce of game feel: screen shake on hits, particles on pickup, squash-and-stretch on jumps. Same mechanic with zero juice feels flat. Same mechanic with great juice feels addictive. Feel is a feature, not decoration.

Feedback must be instant and readable. Every player action needs a response within ~100ms: a sound, a flash, a number pop. If the player wonders 'did that work?', your feedback failed. When in doubt, exaggerate — players forgive too much feedback, never too little.

choices: The sweet spot between boredom and anxiety
cards.explain: Too easy = bored, too hard = anxious. Great difficulty curves keep the player in the channel between them.

choices: Starts brutal to filter weak players
Teaches a skill, tests it, then combines it
questions.explain: Teach, test, combine — the classic ramp. Brutal starts and flat lines both kill engagement.

choices: Choices without downside aren't real choices
questions.explain: Tension needs stakes. If every option is safe, the player is just going through the motions.

choices: Feedback that makes actions feel amazing
questions.explain: Screen shake, particles, squash-and-stretch — juice turns a flat mechanic into an addictive one.
questions.q: What does 'juice' add to a game?

questions.explain: Every action needs an immediate response — sound, flash, pop. Silence makes players doubt the game.

choices: A difficulty spike broke the flow channel
questions.explain: Spikes throw players out of the flow channel into anxiety. Ramps keep them; spikes lose them.
questions.q: A player quits saying 'too hard'. Likely cause?

flashcards.back: How challenge rises over time — it should ramp, never spike or flatline.
Meaningful choices need downside: tension comes from gambling, not from free wins.
The feedback layer — particles, shake, squash — that makes actions feel great.
The zone between boredom and anxiety where players stay fully engaged.

cards.body: In a playtest, say nothing. Don't teach, don't hint, don't defend. Every time you want to intervene, you've just found a design flaw — write it down. The game must teach itself.
cards.title: Watch, don't explain

cards.body: Early: test the core loop with gray boxes — is it fun? Mid: test progression and balance. Late: test polish and onboarding. Testing art style in week one wastes everyone's time.
cards.title: Test the right thing at the right time

cards.body: The 5-player rule: you don't need hundreds of testers. Five players uncover ~85% of usability problems. Watch five, fix, repeat with five fresh players. Ten rounds of five beats one round of fifty.

Kill your darlings. That clever mechanic you love but every tester ignores? Cut it. Players don't care about your effort, only their fun. Every feature must earn its place — if testers skip it, it goes.

choices: You've found a design flaw — write it down
Pause and give them a hint
cards.explain: The urge to explain means the game failed to teach. Silence yourself and fix the game instead.
cards.q: During a playtest, when you want to explain something to the player…

choices: Watch silently — never explain or hint
questions.explain: Explaining masks the flaws you're there to find. The game must teach itself.

choices: Whether the core loop is fun, even in gray box
questions.explain: Fun is foundational and art is expensive. Validate the loop before polishing anything.
questions.q: What should you test first in a new game?

questions.explain: Diminishing returns kick in fast — five fresh players per round, fix, repeat.
questions.q: Why test with only ~5 players per round?

choices: Cut beloved features that testers ignore
questions.explain: Effort doesn't equal fun. If players skip it, it goes — no matter how clever it felt.

choices: Fix the jump — it's a design flaw
questions.explain: Repeated failure at one spot is data, not a skill issue. Tune the challenge; don't blame the tester.
questions.q: A tester keeps dying at the same jump. You should…

flashcards.back: Watch in silence — never explain, hint, or defend. Intervene never.
Five testers find ~85% of usability issues. Fix, then test five fresh players.
Cut features testers ignore, no matter how much you love them.
Early: is the core loop fun? Mid: balance? Late: polish and onboarding.
